title: A hymn in Sorath
hookLine: Guru Tegh Bahadur's hymn of the one who stays level, in pain and in praise

lines: A GOLD RING AND A PINCH OF DUST.
cards: Picture a person who could look at a gold ring and a pinch of dust, side by side on a table, and see no difference worth fighting over. Not because gold is bad, or because they're careless.

Because neither one can move them. A hymn in Sorath describes that person. It's by Guru Tegh Bahadur, the ninth Guru, mahala nine in the headings, and his hymns sit in a group of their own inside Sorath.

teach.h: IN PAIN, NOT TAKING THE PAIN TO HEART.
teach.b: It opens: jo nar dukh mai dukh nahi maanai. In paraphrase: the person who, in pain, does not take the pain to heart. Then the list grows.
Pleasure, affection and fear don't grip them. Gold looks to them like earth. Slander and praise pass over them alike, and so do greed, attachment and pride.
Joy and sorrow, honor and dishonor, they hold all of it lightly. They let go of hoping and craving, and lust and anger can't get a hand on them.
Again and again the list comes in pairs: pain and pleasure, praise and slander, honor and dishonor. The hymn isn't asking for someone who feels nothing.

teach.h: STANDING IN THE MIDDLE OF EACH PAIR.
teach.b: It describes someone who stands in the middle of each pair without being thrown to either end. Then the turn: such a person is the one in whose heart God dwells.

And the closing picture, in paraphrase: Nanak says, the one the Guru has blessed knows this way, and blends with God the way water blends with water. Pour a cup into a river and try to find the cup. That's the calm here.
Not a quiet room. A person so level that nothing pulls them out of shape, and so open that they disappear into God like water into water. The Guru set it in Sorath, the raga of steady faith.

how: Guru Tegh Bahadur's Sorath hymns are sung in kirtan in gurdwaras and at home; this one is known by its opening words, jo nar dukh mai dukh nahi maanai.

games.q: what does “a hymn in sorath” mean?
o: a wedding-horse song in which the body is the mare
Guru Tegh Bahadur's song of a person level in pain and praise
Guru Nanak's lament that opens by blessing the Creator

games.q: what's inside the hymn — tap the pairs.

s: the hymn asks for a person who feels nothing
it describes someone who stands in the middle of each pair without being thrown.
much of the hymn's list comes in pairs
pain and pleasure, praise and slander, honor and dishonor.

games.q: someone praises you lavishly in the morning and slanders you by evening. what does the person in this hymn do?
o: enjoy the praise and fight the slander.
let both pass over them alike.
avoid people so neither can happen.
games.why: the hymn says slander and praise are the same to such a person, and in that heart God dwells. calm, not withdrawal.

practice: Let the breath slow, and notice whatever arrives first: a sound, an ache, a thought about later.
Give it one breath, without pushing it away or feeding it, then let it go on by, like a cup of water poured into a river, and meet the next thing the same way.
If you pray, Waheguru can go with each one as it passes; if not, simply keep letting them pass.

wordCard.voice: A hymn in Sorath. Guru Tegh Bahadur's song of the one who, in pain, does not take the pain to heart, and who blends with God like water with water. Today's word.

orig.note: like water with water: the hymn's closing picture of blending with God.

carryVoice: Your line: calm in sorath. Level in the middle of every pair. Same time tomorrow.
